organism: Respiratory syncytial virus, an RNA pneumovirus named for the syncytia (fused-cell masses) that form when infected cells merge. Two major subtypes circulate, A and B, which are not distinguished separately in routine surveillance reporting.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: In infants and young children, most infections are symptomatic, starting with rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, cough, and decreased appetite; fever can occur early, and very young infants may instead show irritability, decreased activity, or apnea (pauses in breathing over 10 seconds). Disease can turn severe within days, progressing to bronchiolitis or pneumonia; 2%-3% of young infants are hospitalized for RSV, with the highest rates in the first months of life and risk declining with age - most hospitalized children under 2 have no underlying medical condition. In adults, RSV usually causes mild, upper-respiratory-infection-like symptoms (rhinorrhea, sore throat, cough, headache, fatigue, fever) resolving in 1-2 weeks, but in older adults and those with certain medical conditions it can cause pneumonia or exacerbate chronic conditions like asthma, COPD, or heart failure; among unvaccinated adults, disease severity is comparable to COVID-19 and influenza, and recovery often requires follow-up or skilled nursing care after hospital discharge.
epidemiologySummary: RSV spreads person-to-person via respiratory droplets, direct contact, and contaminated fomites. Infected people are typically contagious for 3-8 days, starting 1-2 days before symptom onset. In most of the continental US it follows a seasonal pattern from fall through spring, though jurisdictions with different climates (Alaska, southern Florida, Puerto Rico, and other tropical or subtropical areas) can see meaningfully different timing, and providers there should follow state/local/territorial guidance rather than the general continental-US calendar. Risk factors for severe pediatric disease include young age, prematurity, being American Indian or Alaska Native, and chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease, immunocompromise, severe cystic fibrosis, or neuromuscular disorders affecting airway clearance.
secularTrendsSummary: Before maternal RSV vaccine or infant RSV antibody products existed, RSV caused an estimated 2 million medical encounters, 58,000-80,000 hospitalizations, and 100-300 deaths annually among US children under 5 - making it the leading cause of infant hospitalization. Among US adults 50 and older, annual burden was estimated at about 2.4 million outpatient visits, 1.8 million emergency department visits, and 200,000 hospitalizations. Real-world data from the 2024-2025 season (the first full season with both maternal vaccination and the newer clesrovimab option available) showed nirsevimab 63%-88% effective against ED visits, hospitalization, and ICU admission depending on the surveillance network, and maternal vaccination 54%-79% effective against infant ED visits and hospitalization - CDC continues to monitor effectiveness each season as these are still newly deployed interventions.
vaccineDescription: Three product families now exist, targeting different life stages by different mechanisms, and a patient generally needs only one: (1) maternal vaccination with Pfizer's Abrysvo (a bivalent prefusion F protein subunit vaccine) during pregnancy, whose antibodies cross the placenta to protect the newborn; (2) infant RSV antibody - nirsevimab (Beyfortus, AstraZeneca/Sanofi) or clesrovimab (Enflonsia, Merck) - long-acting monoclonal antibodies that are passive immunization, not vaccines, given directly to the infant; and (3) adult RSV vaccines for older adults - GSK's Arexvy (adjuvanted prefusion F protein subunit), Pfizer's Abrysvo (the same product used maternally, unadjuvanted prefusion F protein subunit), and Moderna's mResvia (mRNA) - with no preferential recommendation among the three.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Maternal: one dose of Abrysvo during weeks 32-36 of gestation, seasonally timed (September through January in most of the continental US) since protection wanes over time and the goal is to protect the infant through their first RSV season; not recommended in a repeat pregnancy after a prior dose. Infants: one dose of nirsevimab or clesrovimab for infants under 8 months born during or entering their first RSV season (October-March) if the mother didn't receive the vaccine, her status is unknown, or the infant was born less than 14 days after her vaccination - ideally given in the first week of life for infants born October-March, or shortly before the season starts (October/November) for infants born April-September; a second-season dose of nirsevimab specifically (not clesrovimab) is recommended for children 8-19 months who remain at increased risk. Older adults: a single dose of any of the three adult vaccines for everyone 75 and older, and for those 50-74 who are at increased risk of severe disease - this is not an annual vaccine, and vaccinated adults are not currently recommended to receive a second dose; ACIP expanded this age-50-74-at-risk recommendation as recently as June 2025, alongside lowering the routine 75+ threshold from what had been 60+.
vaccineEfficacySummary: Maternal vaccination reduced infant RSV lower respiratory tract disease by 57%-82% within 3 months of birth and 51%-69% within 6 months, depending on outcome severity. Nirsevimab reduced medical encounters, hospitalization, and ICU admission by 79%, 81%, and 90% respectively in trial infants under 8 months; clesrovimab showed comparable results (60%, 91%, and 100%). In older adults, all three adult vaccines reduced RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease in trials, though efficacy figures aren't directly comparable across trials due to differing case definitions and follow-up; real-world data found protein-subunit vaccination (Arexvy/Abrysvo) reduced RSV-associated hospitalization by about 75% in the first season after vaccination, similar across the 60-74 and 75+ age bands, with protection lasting at least 2 seasons but waning over time.
contraindicationsSummary: Across all RSV immunization products (maternal and adult vaccines, and the infant monoclonal antibodies), a severe allergic reaction (e.g. anaphylaxis) to a vaccine or product component is the contraindication, and moderate or severe acute illness with or without fever is the precaution - consult each product's own package insert for its specific component list. Product-specific limits matter here: Abrysvo is the only one of the three adult-labeled vaccines also approved for use during pregnancy (32-36 weeks specifically; not recommended after 36 weeks 6 days, at which point the infant should get RSV antibody instead); Arexvy and mResvia are not approved for pregnant women; and none of the adult vaccines or the infant monoclonal antibodies should be given to the wrong population (RSV antibody products are for infants/young children only, not adults; adult vaccines are not given to infants or children).
vaccineSafetySummary: Adult vaccines (Arexvy, Abrysvo, mResvia): common side effects resemble other vaccines - injection-site pain, fatigue, headache, muscle and joint pain. A real safety signal has emerged specifically for the protein-subunit vaccines (Arexvy and Abrysvo): pre-licensure trials found a small number of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) cases within 42 days of vaccination, and post-licensure FDA/CMS data in adults 65+ suggested an increased risk, estimated around 10 excess GBS cases per million vaccinated adults; ACIP and CDC continue to judge that benefits outweigh this risk. The mRNA vaccine (mResvia) showed no GBS cases in pre-licensure trials, though post-licensure data was not yet available as of this chapter's source. Infant RSV antibody products: most common reactions are rash and injection-site reactions, with no significant difference in serious adverse events versus placebo or the older product palivizumab; postmarketing surveillance (FAERS and VSD) has been reassuring. Maternal vaccination during pregnancy: trial data showed more cases of preterm birth and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy among Abrysvo recipients than placebo, though not statistically significant; FDA restricted the approved window to 32-36 weeks specifically to avoid potential preterm-birth risk earlier in pregnancy, and a 2023-2024 season Vaccine Safety Datalink analysis found no increased risk of preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, or stillbirth, but did find a small increased risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy - CDC and FDA continue to monitor this.
vaccineStorageSummary: All RSV immunization products require refrigerated storage at some point in their handling, but with real differences worth checking per product before administering: see Storage and Handling by Product below for specifics on each of the four products (nirsevimab, clesrovimab, Abrysvo, Arexvy, mResvia).
surveillanceSummary: RSV is NOT a nationally notifiable condition in the US. CDC instead tracks it through the National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System (NREVSS), a laboratory-based system monitoring circulation and seasonality, plus hospitalization-focused surveillance networks (including RSV-NET for pediatric data and networks like VISION and the New Vaccine Surveillance Network for real-world vaccine/product effectiveness).

supplementalTopics.title: Storage and Handling by Product
supplementalTopics.summary: Nirsevimab: refrigerate 2C-8C; once removed, use within 8 hours (room temperature 20C-25C permitted for that window); do not freeze, shake, or expose to light. Clesrovimab: refrigerate 2C-8C; once removed, use within 48 hours at room temperature 20C-25C; do not freeze, shake, or expose to light. Pfizer Abrysvo: refrigerate 2C-8C before reconstitution (do not freeze); after reconstitution, store at room temperature 15C-30C (do not refrigerate or freeze) and use within 4 hours. GSK Arexvy: refrigerate 2C-8C before reconstitution, protected from light; after reconstitution, keep refrigerated or at room temperature up to 25C and use within 4 hours, still protected from light. Moderna mResvia: store frozen between -40C and -15C before thawing, protected from light; after thawing, refrigerate 2C-8C for up to 90 days or hold at room temperature up to 25C for 24 hours (do not refreeze or refrigerate after a room-temperature thaw), and if refrigerator-thawed let it reach room temperature for 10-20 minutes before administering.

supplementalTopics.title: Choosing Between Maternal Vaccination and Infant Antibody
supplementalTopics.summary: Most infants need only one of the two options, not both. Maternal vaccination gives the infant immediate protection at birth with no injection for the baby, but may be less effective if the mother is immunocompromised or if the infant is born too soon after vaccination (under 14 days), and carries the small hypertensive-disorder safety signal noted above. Infant RSV antibody delivers antibodies directly rather than relying on transplacental transfer, and its protection may wane more slowly than the maternal vaccine's - but delayed administration can leave a newborn temporarily unprotected, which is why infants born October through March should get it within their first week of life, ideally during the birth hospitalization. Recommended timing is flexible by design to improve access, and jurisdictions with atypical RSV seasonality may issue locally adjusted timing guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Coadministration and Adverse Event Reporting
supplementalTopics.summary: RSV and influenza vaccines may produce a somewhat weaker immune response if given at the same visit, though the clinical significance is unknown; coadministration with all other adult vaccines is otherwise considered acceptable, and there's no required interval between RSV products and other vaccines if not given the same day. Adverse event reporting differs by scenario: if an RSV antibody product (nirsevimab or clesrovimab) is given alone, report suspected adverse events to FDA's MedWatch; if given simultaneously with any vaccine, report to VAERS instead (noting the RSV antibody product in Section 9 of the VAERS form), and no separate MedWatch report is then needed. CDC's V-safe program is also available for vaccine recipients (adults 60+ and pregnant women 16-49) to enroll in active post-vaccination symptom monitoring for 42 days.

keyPoints: Named for the syncytia (fused cell masses) that form in infected tissue
RSV is the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the US, with an estimated 58,000-80,000 hospitalizations annually before newer prevention products existed

Three immunization strategies now exist for three different populations: maternal vaccination (Abrysvo), infant monoclonal antibodies (nirsevimab/Beyfortus or clesrovimab/Enflonsia), and older-adult vaccines (Arexvy, Abrysvo, or mResvia) - most patients need only one
As of June 2025, ACIP recommends adult vaccination for all adults 75+ and adults 50-74 at increased risk - both age thresholds were recently expanded from the original 60+ recommendation

A confirmed Guillain-Barre syndrome safety signal exists specifically for the two protein-subunit older-adult vaccines (Arexvy, Abrysvo), estimated at about 10 excess cases per million vaccinated adults 65+; the mRNA vaccine (mResvia) has not shown this signal so far
The RSV vaccine for older adults is a single lifetime dose for now, not an annual vaccine - CDC is still monitoring whether booster doses will eventually be needed
RSV is not a nationally notifiable disease; CDC tracks it through laboratory surveillance (NREVSS) and hospitalization networks (RSV-NET and others) instead
Self-attestation of a risk factor is sufficient for adult RSV vaccination eligibility - providers should not require medical documentation
